distribution-consequences-s1.title: Land, farmland and people in three countries

table.caption: Population, land and farmers in Countries X, Y and Z (invented data for practice)

distribution-consequences-s2.title: A notice from the health office of an invented province
distribution-consequences-s2.text:
Invented for practice. Notice from the Northern Hills Health Office, Country A, March 2026:

Our province has about 6 people per square kilometer. Villages are far apart, and some families now drive two hours to the nearest hospital. Two small clinics will close this year because each served fewer than 300 patients. A mobile clinic will visit each valley once a month. Meanwhile, the Capital Region, with over 1,000 people per square kilometer, is building a third hospital because its emergency rooms are full.

items.q: Use the table. What is the arithmetic density of Country X, in people per square kilometer?

mistakes.why: You divided by arable land. That gives physiological density. Arithmetic density uses all the land.
You used farmers and arable land. That is agricultural density. Arithmetic density is all people over all land.

why.correct: Arithmetic density is total population divided by total land area: $\frac{40{,}000{,}000}{400{,}000} = 100$ people per km².

items.q: Use the table. What is the physiological density of Country Y, in people per square kilometer of arable land?

mistakes.why: You divided by all the land. Physiological density divides by arable land, the land that can grow crops.
You used only the farmers. Physiological density counts the whole population.

why.correct: Physiological density is total population divided by arable land: $\frac{40{,}000{,}000}{400{,}000} = 100$ people per km² of arable land.

items.q: Which country has the highest physiological density, and what does that suggest?
options: Country X: it has the most farmers of the three countries
Country Y: it has the most land and the most arable land of the three
Country Z: its farmland must feed the most people per km²
Countries X and Y: they have the same number of people

why.correct: Physiological density compares people with arable land. Country Z has 2,000 people per km² of arable land, the most pressure on its farmland of the three.
options: X has the most farmers, which raises agricultural density, not physiological density (1,000 per km²).
a large area of arable land lowers physiological density; Y has 100 per km².
Right: Z has 10 million people on 5,000 km² of arable land, 2,000 per km².
the same population on different amounts of farmland gives different physiological densities.

items.q: Country Y has the lowest agricultural density. What does this most likely show about farming in Country Y?
options: Country Y has too little farmland to feed its people
Most people in Country Y work on farms
Country Y has passed the number of people its land can support
Few farmers work each km² of farmland, likely with many machines on large farms

why.correct: Agricultural density is farmers per km² of arable land. A low value, like Country Y’s 5, usually means large farms that use machines and few workers. A high value, like Country X’s 500, often means many small farms worked by hand.
options: Y has the most arable land of the three; low agricultural density is about farmers, not food supply.
only 2 million of Y’s 40 million people are farmers.
agricultural density does not measure how many people the land can support.
Right: agricultural density counts farmers per km² of arable land; a low value means few workers per km².

items.q: A student says, "Country Z has the highest densities, so it has passed its carrying capacity." Why does the table NOT support this claim?
options: Carrying capacity depends on technology, resources and trade, which the table does not show
Country Z has the fewest farmers, so its density is low
Carrying capacity is the same thing as arithmetic density
Density cannot be calculated from a population and a land area

why.correct: Carrying capacity is the number of people an area can support without harming it. It depends on technology, water, soil and trade. A high density does not prove a place has passed its carrying capacity: the Netherlands is very dense and well fed.
options: Right: density measures crowding; carrying capacity is how many people an area can support.
Z has the highest arithmetic and physiological densities in the table.
this is the mix-up the question is about; they are different ideas.
it can: arithmetic density is population divided by land area.

items.q: According to the notice, how does low density affect health care in the Northern Hills?
options: Hospitals are overcrowded because so many people live close together
Clinics serve few patients each, so some close and people travel far for care
Health care is easier to reach because the roads have little traffic
The province is building a third hospital to meet demand

why.correct: Where few people live far apart, each clinic serves few patients and costs more per person, so services close or become mobile. The passage gives the evidence: closures and two-hour drives.
options: that describes the Capital Region in the notice, not the Northern Hills.
Right: the notice says clinics with few patients close and families drive two hours.
the notice says people now drive two hours to a hospital.
the Capital Region is building the third hospital.

items.q: Which statement correctly compares the two provinces in the notice?
options: Both provinces have too few patients to keep their clinics open
The Capital Region has fewer people per square kilometer than the Northern Hills
Low density makes services hard to reach in the Northern Hills, while high density overloads them in the Capital Region
Density has no effect on health care in either province

why.correct: A compare speaks of both sides. Low density spreads patients thin in the Northern Hills; high density crowds hospitals in the Capital Region.
options: the Capital Region’s emergency rooms are full.
the notice says over 1,000 in the capital and about 6 in the Northern Hills.
Right: this speaks of both provinces and links each problem to density.
the notice links clinic closures and full hospitals to how many people live nearby.

items.q: At what scale of analysis does the notice describe health care?
options: National: the whole of Country A as one unit
Global: countries around the world
Regional: a world region of several countries
Local (subnational): two provinces of one country

why.correct: The data describe provinces inside one country, so the scale of analysis is local (subnational).
options: the notice gives values for provinces, not one value for the country.
only one country, Country A, appears.
there is only one country in the notice, and it compares its provinces.
Right: the notice compares provinces inside Country A.

items.q: Which measure divides a country’s total population by its arable land?
options: Physiological density
Arithmetic density
Agricultural density
Carrying capacity

why.correct: Physiological density = total population ÷ arable land. It shows the pressure people put on the land that feeds them.
options: Right: it compares people with land that can grow crops.
arithmetic density divides by all land, not arable land.
agricultural density divides only the farmers by arable land.
carrying capacity is how many people an area can support, not a ratio of people to land.

items.q: Egypt has a moderate arithmetic density but a very high physiological density. What explains the difference?
options: Most Egyptians work as farmers
Only a few percent of Egypt’s land can grow crops, almost all of it along the Nile
Egypt has more land that can grow crops than most countries
Egypt’s population is spread evenly over its desert

why.correct: Arithmetic density spreads Egypt’s people over all its land, including empty desert. Physiological density counts only arable land, which is about 3 percent of Egypt (World Bank, 2021 data), so its value is far higher.
options: that would raise agricultural density; the gap here comes from how little land is arable.
Right: most of Egypt is desert, so a small area of farmland feeds a large population.
it is the reverse: Egypt has very little arable land.
Egypt’s people are clustered along the Nile.

items.q: Bangladesh has more than 1,000 people per km² of land, and Canada has about 4 (World Bank, 2022). Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Bangladesh has passed its carrying capacity and Canada has not
Canada has more farmers per km² of farmland than Bangladesh
Bangladesh’s land is far more crowded than Canada’s overall
Most of Canada’s land is crowded with people

why.correct: The figures are arithmetic densities: people per km² of all land. They show crowding, not whether a place can feed its people.
options: density alone cannot show carrying capacity; it depends on food, technology and trade.
arithmetic density says nothing about farmers.
Right: arithmetic density compares people with all the land.
Canada’s low average hides large, nearly empty areas in the north.

items.q: The Netherlands has one of the highest population densities in Europe, yet it grows a large surplus of food for export. Which idea does this best show?
options: Agricultural density and carrying capacity are the same measure
Physiological density is low wherever farms export food
Dense countries have to buy their food from other countries
High density does not mean an area has passed its carrying capacity

why.correct: Carrying capacity depends on technology and how land is used, so it differs from density. The Netherlands is crowded but its very productive farms keep it well within what its land and trade can support.
options: they are different: one counts farmers per km² of farmland, the other people an area can support.
exports depend on how productive farms are, not on that ratio.
the Netherlands is dense and still exports large amounts of food.
Right: technology and trade can let a crowded country feed itself and others.

items.q: A government plans to build a new hospital. Its province has very low density, with villages far apart. Which problem is most likely?
options: Many patients would live far from the hospital, so travel times would be long
The hospital would be too crowded on its first day of opening
Housing near the hospital would become too expensive for workers
There would be too much traffic on roads near the hospital

why.correct: Low density raises the cost of services per person and the distance to them. High density brings crowding, traffic and high housing costs.
options: Right: low density spreads people out, so a single hospital is far from many of them.
crowding is a problem of high density.
high housing prices are usually a problem of crowded places.
heavy traffic comes with high density.

items.q: Which are likely effects of very high population density in a city? Select all that apply.
options: Crowded public transport and roads
Pressure on water supply and waste systems
Long travel distances to the nearest school
Clinics closing because too few patients live nearby
More land per person for homes and gardens

why.correct: High density crowds roads and transit and strains water and waste systems. Low density brings the opposite problems: long distances and services with too few users.
options: Right: many people share the same space and routes.
Right: more people per km² use more water and make more waste in one place.
High density usually puts schools close by.
That is an effect of low density.
High density means less land per person.

items.q: Build an explanation of one effect of population density in a named place.

specific.frame: In ___, a very high physiological density means ___, so ___.
specific.model: In Egypt, a very high physiological density means a small area of farmland along the Nile must feed a large population, so the country buys much of its wheat from other countries.

place.label: Place
options: Egypt
a desert country

why.1: name a real place; "a desert country" is too vague.

cause.label: What the measure shows
options: a small area of farmland must feed a large population
there are many people

why.1: physiological density is about people per km² of farmland, so say so.

effect.label: Effect
options: the country buys much of its wheat from other countries
the country is crowded

why.1: "crowded" restates the cause; give an effect it leads to.

why.correct: An explanation links the measure to an effect: high physiological density means little farmland per person, so food must come from trade.

items.q: Why is physiological density often a better measure than arithmetic density of the pressure a population puts on its land?
options: It counts only the farmers, who do most of the work on the land
It is the number of people an area can support with its technology
It uses all the land in the country, including the cities
It counts only land that can grow crops, so deserts and ice do not lower it

why.correct: Physiological density compares people with arable land, so it shows how much farmland each person depends on. Arithmetic density can make a desert country look empty when its farmland is crowded.
options: that is agricultural density.
that is carrying capacity, not a density.
arithmetic density uses all the land; physiological uses arable land.
Right: arithmetic density spreads people over land that cannot feed them.

items.q: Order the three densities of Country X in the table from largest to smallest. (Population 40 million, land 400,000 km², arable land 40,000 km², farmers 20 million.)
options: Physiological density (1,000 per km²)
Agricultural density (500 per km²)
Arithmetic density (100 per km²)

why.correct: Physiological: 40 million ÷ 40,000 = 1,000. Agricultural: 20 million ÷ 40,000 = 500. Arithmetic: 40 million ÷ 400,000 = 100.
